did_you_know.text: Did you know? This chapter describes the renewal of the relationship between the LORD and Israel: the LORD promises to be Israel’s God, and Israel will be his people.
Did you know? The LORD’s love for Israel is described as “everlasting love,” so he continues to draw the people to himself with kindness.

Did you know? The gathering of Israel from the lands of exile includes the blind, the lame, pregnant women, and women in labor—a description emphasizing that the return is intended for the entire people, including the weak and vulnerable.
Did you know? The return to Zion is described not only as a return to a place, but also as an abundance of grain, wine, olive oil, sheep, and cattle, and as a life free from worry.

Did you know? Rachel is portrayed as weeping for her children and refusing to be comforted, but immediately afterward the LORD promises that her work will be rewarded and that her children will return from the land of the enemy.
Did you know? Ephraim is portrayed in the chapter as a precious son and a delightful child, and the LORD declares: “I will surely have compassion on him.”
Did you know? The LORD promises to sow the house of Israel and the house of Judah again—“the seed of humans and the seed of animals”—as an image of renewal and fertility in the land.
Did you know? The chapter presents a principle of personal responsibility: each person will die for their own sin, not because of their ancestors’ sin.
Did you know? Jeremiah describes a promise of a “new covenant” with the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
Did you know? In the new covenant, the law is not described merely as an external command: the LORD promises to place it within the people and write it on their hearts.
